Mesh is a local network topology (the logical arrangement of nodes, such as computers, servers, and routers, and links, such as cables, wires, and wireless connections) where nodes are connected through different means to other nodes.\n\nEssentially, it is an interconnected network of devices that send, pass, and receive data packages.
As many as you want! Every device serves a purpose, so if you aren\'t using it to send or receive data, your device will act as a middleman so no node is wasted!
Why is it better than Wi-Fi? And when is it best applied?

Unlike Wi-Fi, which relies on a single broadcast point (like radio and TV), Mesh is decentralized, acting as an expansive "spiderweb." It means that:

• Wi-Fi weakens as you distance yourself from the router, whereas in Mesh, it is a 'blanket' of coverage supported by many nodes. It is the truest form of Seamless Roaming.
• Wi-Fi has a single point of possible failure while Mesh is supported by multiple nodes. Meaning, if one node fails, another one reroutes the path, taking its place seamlessly. This is referred to as Self-Healing.
• Wi-Fi requires direct connection and manually switching between bands, whereas Mesh is controlled and gives you connection to the network via a single app, which is roaming as you move around. This also means constant internet speeds wherever you are.
• Wi-Fi is far easier to install in 'dead zones' or areas that lack traditional internet connection. Instead of setting up wired connections and hardware, you can simply plug any form of node (even a printer works) into an outlet and that area gets access to the whole Mesh network! So long as the node can send and receive, it works.

Summary: Wi-Fi is best in small-scale use, like around your house or office. But in terms of city-wide usage, Mesh is far more ideal.

• For Mesh used in the home or residence sense, it is no different from connecting to a traditional router. Simply open the app, enter the password (once), and join the Mesh network (there may be multiple options).\n• For a greater Mesh network, the exact same premise follows. Simply connect to a node in the network via an app and you\'re golden. Anything you send will go where it needs to.

To disconnect, it is simply a matter of what you want to disconnect.

• A phone would mean you simply toggle off the Mesh network via the app. A computer would mean the same. And if you ever wanted to forget that network, simply choose "Forget This Network" on either device.
• For hardware, like a node you plug in or any electrical device, you can simply unplug it from any electrical source. The Mesh will not suffer for it!

Mesh exercises end-to-end encryption via keys. This is utilized on all internet traffic, meaning outsiders cannot see what you are browsing or the messages you are sending or receiving. Essentially, it is as safe as any safe system out there.

As for names, like your SSID or network, unless you explicitly place your social security number on there for all to see, you will be fine.

The only exception may be that your device will have a node number that will be visible to other nodes in the system, and if you utilize any location applications like GPS, either your coordinates or your node number will be shared with other nodes.

For the device hosting the hotspot, you can choose between 2GHz and 5GHz:
• 2GHz: Longer distances and deeper penetration of obstacles (walls and furniture).
• 5GHz: Faster speeds with less range and penetration.

Otherwise, this depends on whether you are referring to your phone or between nodes:
• A phone's range is dependent on the device's Bluetooth distance frequency. However, average max distances on Bluetooth connections can vary between 50 and 150 feet. This is the distance between your phone and a node in the Mesh network.
• Between node to node: This is limited to the amount of physical hardware available: antennas, electrical power, obstacles. The frequency band you use, 2.4–5GHz or sub-GHz, will determine if the range is similar to that of Bluetooth or miles in distance.

• If you have a non-mobile node, then your battery life is dependent on you charging your device, whether it be in a public, private, residential or commercial location.\n• For a mobile device, like your phone, as long as you remain connected to the Mesh network, your device is actively participating in the entire system. This means that if you aren\'t sending or receiving, your device can act as a \'middleman\', moving data packets along a predetermined path. This can and will exhaust battery life. The best solution would be to disconnect and reconnect only when you need to.

Whenever!

• Disasters: Mesh being decentralized from city infrastructure means that it can give rescuers and first responders constant and instant access to the Mesh network. As long as a portable node is in the area, users can communicate information fast and reliably. And if a user isn't near a portable node, they can simply 'daisy-chain' through other nodes.
• Military: By eliminating the single point of failure in traditional military networks, militaries can rely on the multi-failure system of Mesh that can avoid being jammed or destroyed. This means that at any point, if a node path is interrupted, operations can continue without delay or vital data compromise. This is particularly good for security, drones and electronic warfare.

• Home: The home page is where you set up and initiate your Mesh network OR join another via Wi-Fi Connect, URI link, or QR code.
• Network: This page is where you can view your or other networks in the area. The network name is displayed, along with connection stability, status (on/off), and the number of nodes or 'hops' in the network. This means the number of devices your data will traverse to reach its destination.
• Send: This page is dedicated to sending data, whether it be files, photos, videos, or anything in between. You simply select the file, choose the recipient, then send. It creates a list of data sent, so you can keep track of what you've sent, when, and to whom.
• Receive: This page is all about what gets sent to YOU! It creates a list based on the date and order received. You can choose to either download them to your gallery, send them elsewhere, or save to a specific folder.
• Chat: This is the place where you have one-on-one conversations with other nodes in the network (other nodes who can receive AND respond. Your toaster can play Doom, but probably not send data ☹️). You have a prelude screen, where you can see multiple conversations, their status and stability, and a preview of the most recent message. When you click a specific device, you enter the chatroom where you can type and read your chats.
• Log: Record of every procedure kept in jargon (technical) terms.
• Settings: The place where you can customize the entire application, see where the Project Mesh folder is located, and change the device's name if you so choose.
Can I still use Bluetooth for my headphones?
Can I log back into my chat via another phone?
Sadly no. Your chats can be saved, but they are saved onto the device used. Each node is unique.
Any Android device can use Project Mesh, while any nodes capable of acting as a middleman can operate within the Mesh network.
